headline: Scene Igniter Activity - Short Role-Play Scenes for ESL Speaking
outcomes: Students get an immediate speaking scene with roles, context, and a reason to talk
Role-play feels structured but not scripted, so students can improvise at their level
Equal speaking turns help the teacher avoid one confident student taking over the scene
The activity turns a topic into a memorable moment rather than another abstract discussion question
howItWorks: LessonCaptain generates a short scene connected to your topic, with roles and a simple conflict or task
Students receive or see their assigned roles and prepare a first line or response
The class performs the scene live while the teacher guides timing and turn-taking
The teacher can replay the scene with new language goals, stronger emotion, or a different outcome
teacherUseCases: Warm up a speaking lesson with a quick, low-stakes role-play
Practise functional English such as requests, apologies, complaints, advice, or negotiation
Give one-on-one students a structured conversation without inventing a scenario from scratch

faq.a: It gives students the setup and roles, but the language is not fully scripted. Students still produce their own lines, which keeps the activity communicative.
Yes. In a one-on-one lesson, the teacher can take one role and the student takes the other, or the student can practise multiple responses in the same scene.

faq.q: Which situations make strong Scene Igniter prompts?
faq.a: Everyday conflict, travel, customer service, work situations, school life, and social decisions all work well because students immediately understand what the characters want.
It can run from the shared teacher screen, and students can also use devices for role assignment in a live LessonCaptain session.

faq.q: How do I make the language more challenging?
faq.a: Raise the difficulty, add a function such as persuasion or compromise, or rerun the scene with a new constraint like 'be more polite' or 'use three target phrases'.
